newsitem.title: USA: Environmental group urges protection of Idaho forests.
newsitem.headline: Environmental group urges protection of Idaho forests.

text.p: An environmental group called on the U.S. Forest Service Wednesday to halt timber sales and road construction on unspoiled national forest lands in Idaho, saying development was putting these areas at risk.
The Wilderness Society issued a report that found there had been "a dramatic decline in the amount of roadless land in Idaho's national forests."
The report said that Idaho had more wild, primitive land than any state except Alaska.

But in little more than a decade, the area of roadless land in Idaho's national forests had dropped by about one million acres (400,000 hectares), according to the report called "Idaho's vanishing wild lands."

The report, the result of a two-year study, warned that if the Forest Service continued to eliminate roadless areas at the same rate, all of Idaho's remaining 7 million acres (2.8 million hectares) of unprotected roadless land would be gone in about 70 to 100 years.
"Idaho is rapidly losing the very wilderness values that make it such an important part of the nation's natural heritage," Wilderness Society president William Meadows said.

"The destruction of one million acres over the last decade represents an irreversible loss of clean water, prime fish and wildlife habitat, scenic countryside and backcountry recreational opportunities," he said in a statement.

In addition to the unprotected, roadless land, Idaho has 4.1 million acres (1.7 million hectares) of federal land that Congress has designated as wilderness. But it has been 17 years since Congress last protected any federal wild lands from development in Idaho, The Wilderness Society said.

Craig Gehrke, The Wilderness Society's Idaho regional director, said roads have had a devastating impact on water quality and fish habitats. "They've also fragmented forests and damaged or destroyed important wildlife habitat," he said.
The Wilderness Society singled out 10 areas of national forest in Idaho that it said were in "imminent danger of destruction from logging, road construction and related development."
The society, a non-profit organisation with more than 250,000 members, recommended that the Clinton administration declare a moratorium on development in roadless areas.
It urged the Forest Service to immediately stop timber sales, road construction, and other activities that harmed roadless areas in Idaho.
It said authorities should adopt a plan to protect roadless areas larger than 1,000 acres (400 hectares).
The society's report said that, in the long run, Congress should adopt comprehensive wilderness legislation to make Idaho the premier wilderness state outside Alaska.
A Forest Service spokesman in Washington had no immediate comment.
